### On Education and Learning Attitudes
Feb 1976   p.21-29
Education, to be adequately defined, is any process by which an individual acquires knowledge of the Universe and perspective on life, accompanied by the reciprocal and rational development of precepts and personality, with its dichotomous modes — formal and informal education. It proffers a fascinating and perpetually interesting inquiry into the nature of our existence and our universe.
The prevalent vista of contemporary philosophers and the public masses on the purpose of education is twofold, namely, the social purpose and the individual purpose. They affirm that its social aim is to cultivate each individual so that one can become a beneficial member of society by inheriting the collective human experience and civilizations. They also assert that its individual purpose is to furnish him with dexterity to handle new experience efficiently, so as to lead a more successful and productive life. Instead of acquiescing to their doctrines, I would say that these are not the purposes of education, but rather, they are only the consequences of education. The authentic, ultimate goal of education is for the quest and pursuit of Truth and knowledge of our cosmos, as well as to discern and apprehend life. Besides, education should be directed towards the beatitude and welfare of mankind.
There are, I would say, six momentous consequential aspects of formal education - education at schools: faith, character, intellect, aesthetics, ethics and labour.
Education for faith fosters in us confidence, hope and trust in ourselves, our friends, our world and our understanding of the Universe. These traits will, in turn, heave us a secure feeling, even when we encounter frustrations and failures in the course of our life. It is plain that the human race will  extinct without faith, for we cannot love, we cannot trust, and we cannot cooperate.
Education for character is perhaps the most significant of all these consequential aspects, for it really points to education for individuality and identity. It requires us to develop character aptly and correctly. Life is like a drama; each actor or actress plays a specific character in it. Thus, this drama will have no meaning at all if there is no differentiation of characters. Analogously, life has no meaning at all if intellectual education does not provide us with the faculty of intelligence and alertness, so that we can think logically and act rationally. Human civilization is indispensable with intellectual education, for without it the cumulative knowledge and experience of mankind cannot be inherited.
Aesthetic education initiates our capability of appreciating the beauty and pulchritude of Nature and our arts. This aesthetic feeling, together with love, constitutes the purest and most loftiest forms of human emotions. Ethical education promotes our understanding towards inter-human relationships and moral concepts; thus permitting us to gauge our criterion for behaviour and actions, while education for  labour inspires us to work assiduously and honestly. Here, it should be emphasized that these consequential aspects of education can only be achieved through correct concepts and just approaches to education.
The rapid upheaval of science and technology in the last few decades, together with the unprecedented rate of increase in population, in consequence of the triumphs in medical science, have a profound and penetrating impact on our modern society. Mankind, after practising  classical education for centuries, has to reconcile to this abstruse social and psychological veer drastically by adopting new methods in education. The so-called technological revolution produces an accruing differentiation of labour and tasks in our community. In order to cope with this augmenting division of tasks, modern mass educationists have to employ 'pragmatic-mass' education.   It is tragic to see that current educators, instead of stressing on all-round development, tend to condition people to undertake different chores according to their capabilities and intelligence. Moreover, they emphasize too much applied science, social science and practical arts, for they claim that education is for the comfort and welfare of mankind, and these subjects provide comfort for man, they should be emboldened.  Consequently, the study of pure science and fine arts in the last few decades is severely cut, as exemplified by the abrupt curtail of the budget for space program of NASA.
Modern educationists, besides utilizing  sophisticated educational aids and tools for formal education, also employ television, newspapers and magazines as influential mass media. Among these, television is perhaps the most influenctial medium.  It exters a recondite but weighty impellent on average peopel by the  weighty impact on average people by the ideas and concepts underlying its programmes. Hence the ideas on life and the Universe conveyed to the public should be aimed at the TRUE happiness and GOODNESS of the masses; otherwise, the people will gradually lose their foresight and become pragmatic and materialistic (in this context, means vain). I will not deny that current TV programmes (in Hong Kong) are mostly taking the negative trend, I will even say that this negative trend in mass education, coupled with pragmatism and venality, will be disastrous to our world in the near future — and, worst of all, will jeopardize and exterminate humanity, which is an intrinsic character of being man. Moreover, this negative trend tends to suppress free thinking, so that each member of society shall conform himself to prevalent social conventions. Surly men will become the promiscuous hedonistic— practical and pneumatic Alphas, Betas, Gammas and Epsilons, as prognosticated in _Brave New World_!
Through a circumspect contemplation, one can resolve the inherent motives of learning into two categories — the aesthetic, magnanimous attitude, and the egoistic, futile attitude. The former is a virtue aided by integrity and genteelness, while the latter is necessarily an iniquity, by its mercenariness and egoism. The aesthetic, magnanimous  attitude is the inevitable vehemence that motivates the zest and quest for truth and knowledge, which in turn animates the fervour for life. People holding this view are altruistic/philanthropic and sensible; they are liberal, candid and adventurous. Contrariwise, those who always think about their future well-being and self-interest are egocentric, obdurate, insidious and fraudulent. They are phlegmatic towards life. They only have transient interest in persons whom they thought to be beneficial and advantageous to them and to the fields of knowledge they study.  Consequently, these people are detrimental to our society and  our world.
It is facile to see that most of the people in our society are holding this negative view to a considerable extent— and this idea, I would say, is mainly inherited from the last generation (in early education), and formed from the deep impact of our highly competitive environment. In order to abate this undesirable attitude, we must emancipate ourselves from conventional ideas, public opinions and traditions first. Well, I do not mean we have to eradicate or abandon traditions thoroughly — what I mean is to ponder on them carefully before we accept them; otherwise, they have to be modified. Many people accept tradition as their _a priori_ principles of life without question, even after years of 'education', being unaware of the bane and ravage they cause. They tend to concede as what the general public thinks is true, so it is necessary for us to consider public opinion scrupulously before acceptance.  Besides, we must develop our willpower, determination and mental faculty to meet with this problem.
Real education consists in individualized perception, insight and perspicuity into our existence and our Universe. However, the objective aspect of education is also stressed — scientific methods of analysis should be encouraged. It is an acute process by which intuition and self-awareness are stressed so as to promote creativity.  It also provides us with the purest form of human satisfaction - epistemic satisfaction and 'curiosity' satisfaction.
The fundamental role of educational institutions, colleges and universities is to promote and enrich people's zest for life, with emphasis on social and individual responsibilities.  Democracy, righteousness and honesty should be inspired. Extra-curricular inter-collegiate activities should be encouraged.  Considerable freedom should be given to the students so that they can develop their characters freely and naturally. Strict discipline is not advisable, for it may strangle the moral and psychological development of the student. The pupils should be allowed to enunciate their regulations and rules for behavior through rational analysis. They should, in turn, respect the school authority and their freedom.  Moreover, excessive competition and enmity between students should be eliminated. On the whole, educational institutions should set their ideals at the rummage of authentic humanity of mankind.  Arts and science should be studied on an equiponderant  basis.
The study of arts should include the following subjects: history, geography, mathematics, literature, poems, music and language. History, in its widest sense,  is that branch of knowledge which deals with the chronological aspect and rational analysis of human cultural evolution, the study of which can be divided into three main parts, namely, anthropological, chronological and analytical. Of these, the former and the latter are of great importance, for they assist us to look at man's civilizations and human entities from a more 'scientific' basis, in which cultural and mental evolution are perceived in relation to the social, economical and technological background. Geography is that branch of knowledge dealing with the structure of the Earth and people living in it, in which we gain a general knowledge of our land and the people living in it. Mathematics provide us with the faculty of thinking, so that we can contemplate rationally. Literature, music and poems refine our taste and initiate our aesthetic pleasure. The study of language serves as a means of communication so that we can interchange ideas and feelings. The study of science is somewhat much more unified — it should include astronomy, physics, chemistry, biology and other related sciences.
Perhaps our present generation has the loftiest responsibility that any generation ever had. We are successors of our future-dreading society, haunted by energy crisis, population explosion, food crisis, nuclear warfare, crimes, etc. Many people, as a result, lose their faith and zest for life, resorting themselves to egoism, which will consequently eventuate in chaos and tumult in our present society. It is our very task to extricate these evil insights into life.  We must endeavour towards beatitude, truth, pulchritude and humanity. Through education, love, faith and ourselves, let us strive for our ultimate goals — now!
